1.pericope_label: Children, obey your parents: the first commandment with promise

schools.summary: Observe that the apostle shortens his exhortation and drops all high subjects because he is speaking to tender understandings, offering long life rather than the kingdom as what a child most wants to hear; and guard the saying about loving father or mother by insisting on the words more than me, since earthly fathers are to be disobeyed only where they contradict the Father in heaven.

Ask why obedience is commanded where honour has the wider sense, and answer that obedience is the evidence of the debt and the harder part, since the mind recoils from subjection; extend the terms to adopted and illegitimate children, step-parents, guardians and every ancestor, and to the maintenance of aged parents; and explain that Paul dropped the mention of Canaan because its peculiar distinction lasted only till the coming of Christ.
Weigh three ways of construing the words in the Lord — as a limitation on obedience, as the reason for it, or as a specification of the matters in which it is chiefly owed — and prefer the second.

Note that the mother is named particularly as the likelier to be slighted; report that the qualifying clause is absent from several reputable manuscripts, and deny that any child is bound to obey an unreasonable or unscriptural command; and take the promise of long life, though usually fulfilled to dutiful children, in a chiefly spiritual sense under the Christian dispensation.

Meet the difficulty about the first commandment with promise by distinguishing a general declaration attaching to the whole law from a promise annexed to one precept, and confirm it from the grammar against the view that first means first taught; observe that the omission of the words about the land generalises the promise and fixes it on the earth rather than on heaven; and defend the desire for long life as a longer space to prepare for eternity.

debates: Why obedience is commanded where the fifth commandment says honour.
Whether the words in the Lord limit obedience, supply its motive, or specify its matter.
In what sense this is the first commandment with promise, given the mercy promised in the second.
Whether the promised long life is earthly, spiritual, or both.
outliers: Chrysostom alone accounts for the brevity of the passage by the age of those addressed.
Calvin alone asks whether one child in a thousand is found obedient.
Clarke alone reports that the qualifying clause is missing from reputable manuscripts.
Wesley alone reads the promise of long life chiefly in a spiritual sense, against those who fix it on the earth.
Ellicott and Calvin independently rest the same argument on Paul's omission of the words about the land.

4.pericope_label: Fathers and children, masters and servants: correction, nurture, and the limits of bondage

schools.summary: Catalogue the provocations a father offers by word and by deed, down to spending the estate and leaving the children nothing; warn that harshness makes children throw off the yoke while the word for bringing up conveys gentleness, and observe Paul drawing the rein again against indulgence; describe ancient slavery exactly — perpetual, purchased, with the power of life and death protected by law — and deny that the gospel procured any carnal freedom.

Distinguish correction from punishment by their motives, revenge against affectionate concern, and hold that cruel parents generally have bad children; name fathers rather than mothers as the likelier to be severe; and call slavery among Christians an enormity for which perdition has scarcely an adequate punishment, while still binding the Christian slave to serve faithfully the man whose money bought him.

Argue that if obedience is required the commands must be obeyable; divide over the two words for education, whether both carry the severity of ancient discipline and the first means chastening, or whether the wider sense of a child's general culture is supported by the papyri; find the limitation of slavery in the words according to the flesh, since it cannot touch the spirit and the slave is no living tool; and read eyeservice as an indictment of the institution, since only religion removes the need for drivers, and its prevalence would free the slave.

Note that servants are addressed last because last in rank, yet in a more advanced way than the children, with a promise held out in the world to come rather than in this; and tell them not to grieve, since slavery is nothing but a name and a mastership according to the flesh is brief.

Expect that teaching masters and servants their duties would lessen the evils until slavery was rooted out by the influence of Christianity, since both are fellow-servants in respect of Christ, and that even the meanest drudgery done from duty will be rewarded.

debates: What provokes children to wrath, and whether the fault lies in the act or in the motive behind it.
Whether the word rendered nurture means chastening or the whole culture of a child.
Whether the New Testament tolerates slavery, limits it, or condemns it while requiring obedience within it.
Whether the institution was expected to end by the gradual influence of Christianity or by the direct force of the gospel.
outliers: Clarke alone condemns slavery among Christians as a crime beyond adequate punishment while upholding the slave's duty to the man who bought him.
Barnes alone turns the command against eyeservice into an argument about why slaveholding requires drivers.
Calvin alone points out that the apostle tightens the rein immediately after slackening it.
Ellicott alone claims that the phrase of the Lord gradually softened the paternal authority of Roman law.
Robertson alone appeals to papyri and inscriptions against the narrower sense of the word for nurture.

7.pericope_label: Serving with good will, the recompense of the deed, and what masters owe

schools.summary: Forbid the master to infer from the slave's submission either that the slave thinks him right or that religion approves him, since it approves slavery no more than it sanctioned Nero by requiring the martyrs to submit; state that religion is the friend of human rights and would restore every man to freedom; trace the destruction of slavery to the conception of the slave as the Lord's freeman; press the wording that a man receives the deed itself rather than its reward, since a slave in law had neither rights nor hope; and read the ban on threatening as forbidding a man to be driven like a beast.

Set the command against the suppressed indignation of slaves who obey with reluctance, and match the number of injunctions to the number of vices the ancients record; deny the world's valuation, since God esteems a slave's labour as highly as a king's duties; and hold that though the civil code granted masters vast power, God allows none beyond the law of love — measuring the philosophers, who urge equity but never look past utility, against an apostle who asks what masters owe.

Have punishment lean toward mercy and be as light as possible, with revenge excluded as being of the devil, and take the phrase to mean the relaxing of a threatened penalty; and quote the rabbinic saying that before God women, slaves, the poor and the rich are all alike.

debates: Whether the command to submit implies any approval of the condition submitted to.
What the promise means that a man shall receive what he does, and why it matters that a slave had no standing in law.
Where the limit on a master's power comes from — the civil code, the calculations of utility, or the law of love.
What doing the same things requires of masters in practice.
outliers: Barnes alone forbids the master to draw the pro-slavery inference from the very verse commanding obedience, and compares him to Nero and to Mary.
Ellicott alone credits the abolition of slavery to a conception logically worked out from the epistles.
Calvin alone measures the number of commands against the number of vices recorded of ancient slaves.
Calvin alone faults the philosophers for arguing equity from utility and asking only what suits the householder.
Robertson alone remarks that Paul is afraid neither of capital nor of labour.

10.pericope_label: Be strong in the Lord: the whole armour, and the enemies it is against

schools.summary: Judge the address my brethren an interpolation absent from this epistle and the Colossian; identify the panoply from Polybius, note which pieces Paul omits and adds, and observe that he had been chained to a Roman soldier for years; insist that the armour must be complete, since one unguarded point may be fatal, and that to put it on is to put on Christ; prefer the order blood and flesh, lest the struggle be confused with one against the flesh within; and trace the word for world-ruler through Orphic, Gnostic, rabbinic and imperial usage.

Rest an argument on the address soldiers use to one another in the field; press the strangeness of the phrase, as though might itself would not serve without its exertion; take the panoply for the equipment of the heavy troops who stormed cities, and the wiles for the devil's methods, a man's way of sinning being Satan's way of ruining him; render the phrase as the spiritualities of wickedness, falsehood in the garb of truth; report the view that the rulers of this darkness are the Jewish authorities; and distribute the evil powers between a citadel and the provinces.

Frame the passage as a warfare with a captain, a banner and rules of war, requiring a soldier both stout-hearted and well armed, since armour without a good heart within will stand a man in little stead.

Raise the objection that a strength men cannot supply is uselessly enjoined, and answer that the sentence both exhorts to courage and directs them to ask God for what they lack; picture the negligent soldier who takes his helmet and forgets his shield, or leaves his arms hanging on the wall; and set the exactness of human combat against a conflict where no human power avails, drawing from it a caution against revenge.

Read the armour through the anointing of forehead, ears, nostrils and breast, so that those who have put on the breastplate of righteousness stand against the wiles of the devil as Christ went out after his baptism and vanquished the adversary.

debates: Whether the words my brethren belong to the text, and what may be built on them.
Why a strength that must be given is nevertheless commanded.
Whether the armour is described from Roman practice, from moral necessity, or from the rites of Christian initiation.
Whether the principalities and powers are spirits or human authorities.
outliers: Wesley alone argues from a word that Ellicott judges to be no part of the text.
Robertson alone lists the pieces Paul omits from and adds to the classical panoply, and explains his knowledge by his captivity.
Clarke alone reports the view that the rulers of this darkness are the rabbins and Jewish rulers.
Wesley alone assigns the evil powers a citadel and provinces.
Calvin alone turns the spiritual nature of the conflict into a warning against revenging human injuries.

13.pericope_label: Withstand in the evil day: the girdle of truth, the breastplate, and the shoes

schools.summary: Render the clause as having conquered all, stand, on the authority of the best Greek writers; observe that the war is perpetual though its violence varies; contrast the armour fabled to be sent by the gods with what Paul describes as real; take the breastplate for the imputed righteousness in which Christ presents us faultless, and note that no armour for the back is named because we always face the enemy; and read the shoes as a readiness to publish the gospel, after the passover eaten with feet shod.

Divide over the same participle, some making it the vanquishing of every foe and one refusing that rendering as against the apostle's usage, so that having done what we are called to do we simply stand firm; doubt whether the reason for assigning truth to the girdle can be determined at all, or else trace both pieces to Isaiah; and work through the senses of the word for preparation, rejecting the preaching of the gospel because each piece is a quality and not a function, and settling on the Septuagint sense of a base.

Refuse to press the details, since an allusion to military custom is all that was intended and it is idle to ask why truth is a girdle rather than a breastplate; reject the imputed sense of righteousness here as out of place where a blameless life is the subject; and reach the Septuagint sense of a base for the shoes, or else take the gospel as what equips us for a journey we are by nature too indolent to make.

Explain that the soldiers had first to be posted in rank and their spirit roused, since a man must be armed within before he is armed without — and for spiritual soldiers there is no arming without at all; and note that the first thing in tactics is to know how to stand.

debates: Whether the words rendered having done all mean having conquered everything or having discharged the duty of the hour.
How far the individual pieces of armour may be interpreted, and whether the assignment of each quality has a reason.
Whether the breastplate of righteousness is imputed righteousness or a blameless life.
What the preparation of the gospel of peace means: preaching it, being ready, or standing on it as a base.
outliers: Ellicott alone rejects the rendering having conquered all, naming Chrysostom among those he sets aside.
Clarke alone contrasts the divinely sent armour of the ancient heroes with the reality Paul describes.
Calvin rejects the imputed sense of righteousness here while Wesley asserts it, reversing the expected confessional alignment.
Wesley alone argues from the absence of armour for the back.
Gill and Ellicott independently settle on the Septuagint sense of a base, against the reading that makes the shoes a readiness to preach.

16.pericope_label: The shield of faith, the helmet, the sword of the Spirit, and prayer

schools.summary: Take above all to mean over all rather than most important, and describe the great oblong shield and the burning arrows it caught; distinguish the patient, almost passive faith meant here from the faith we stand in and from the energetic faith of Hebrews; divide over the helmet, some importing the hope of salvation from the parallel epistle and one insisting that the word means salvation in the concrete and that the verb changes from putting on to receiving; and observe that the sword is the one offensive weapon in the list.

Identify the fiery darts with a leaded missile and suggest that Greek helmets bore emblematic figures, perhaps of hope; grade the hope of salvation from a confidence that God will finish his work up to full assurance of glory; mark that the armour has been defensive until the sword, since we must attack as well as secure ourselves; argue from the structure that prayer is no part of the armour, the catalogue of six being complete; and rebuke those who use only mental prayer and think their worship superior.

Deny that the distinctions can be pressed, faith and the word being one thing since the word is faith's object and faith nothing without it, and then allow that the two most necessary weapons rightly answer to them; take the helmet as the hope that lifts the head toward what is promised; and explain why continuance in prayer is enjoined twice, since in prosperity we feel no excitement to pray and flee to God only when driven by distress.
Offer Daniel among the lions as the proof of what faith does, call it an impalpable buckler against an unseen foe, and show it quenching a dart of base desire by suggesting a picture of the judgment.

debates: Whether above all ranks faith first among the graces or describes how the shield is carried.
Which faith is meant — the faith we stand in, the faith that removes mountains, or a patient trust that endures.
Whether the helmet is the hope of salvation or salvation itself already possessed.
Whether prayer belongs to the armour or stands outside the catalogue as what enables its use.
outliers: Ellicott alone refuses to import the hope of salvation from the parallel epistle, reading the helmet as a present possession.
Ellicott alone names an allegory of his own century as the best commentary on the passage.
Clarke alone argues from the absence of a Grecian counterpart that prayer is no part of the armour.
Calvin alone asks why perseverance in prayer is commanded twice, and answers from the way prosperity dulls it.
Wesley alone rebukes a party who confine themselves to mental prayer as though it were the higher worship.

19.pericope_label: Pray for me: utterance, boldness, an ambassador in chains, and the sending of Tychicus

schools.summary: Infer that no man is so gifted as to need no prayers of his brethren, and ask who could plead exemption better than Paul; deny that his request betrays unbelief or that he was ever silent from fear, the danger being rather that a splendid beginning should not be sustained; reject the forensic sense of the request, since he seeks not the powers of a dexterous sophist to shield himself by false pretences but a clear and strong confession; and admire that a man with death before his eyes provided for the most distant churches.

Take the request for utterance in its legal sense, of permission and power to defend oneself in court, as befits an ambassador expecting a public hearing, and hold that the imprisonment turned to the furtherance of the gospel; and set the pomp in which the ambassadors of men appear against the appearance of the ambassador of Christ.

Correct the rendering so that word is given him in the opening of his mouth, and identify what is sought with the promise that it shall be given in that hour what to speak; explain the single chain as a manacle binding the hand to the guarding soldier, and read it as the badge of an ambassadorial dignity that ought to have exempted him; note that the word for ambassador comes from the word for an old man; and extend the call to prayer from Paul to every prisoner and slave, counted by the thousand and the million.

Observe that a man once called Mercury for his command of language still asks the churches to pray for utterance, and find three requests in the verse — release from restraint, fitness of expression, and boldness to deliver the whole counsel of God.

debates: Why an apostle should need the prayers of his converts, and whether asking betrays any distrust.
Whether the utterance sought is a legal defence, an inspired word, or plain courage.
What the single chain signifies, and how an ambassador comes to wear one.
Why Tychicus was sent, and what a prisoner owed to distant churches.
outliers: Clarke alone gives the request for utterance a forensic sense, and Calvin alone rejects that sense as asking for the arts of a sophist.
Ellicott alone reconstructs the chain as a wrist manacle and observes that the guard may not always have troubled to hold it.
Barnes alone turns the verse into a census of the prisoners and slaves of his own country and a call to pray for them.
Henry alone notes that the man asking for utterance had been taken for the god of eloquence.
Robertson alone derives the title of ambassador from the word for an old man and applies it to Paul's age.

22.pericope_label: Tychicus sent, peace to the brethren, and grace to all who love Christ incorruptibly

schools.summary: Report the dispute whether the letter went to Ephesus or to Laodicea, and concede that the objection from its naming no person there has not been successfully answered; require the genuineness of love to be shown in holiness of life, against those who profess to know Christ and in works deny him; take the closing word both of not corrupting the gospel and of having no corrupt affections; and note that the final Amen is missing from several of the best copies, and that it implies the faithfulness of the promiser rather than a wish.

Find in the generality of the benediction — the brethren, and all who love the Lord — a difference from the personal address of every other epistle that would be inexplicable if it were written to Ephesus alone; identify the salutation of grace as the apostle's own handwritten token; insist that the closing word means incorruptibility, ordinarily used of the immortality of heaven, so that the love meant is imperishable; and judge the subscription itself to be without authority though probably correct here.

Weigh whether peace here is the ordinary salutation or concord among themselves and prefer the second, since the prayer shows love and faith no less than peace to be gifts bestowed through Christ; and read incorruption of the lover, since a heart free from hypocrisy is free from corruption — turning the point against those who profess religion while holding low notions of Christ and worshipping him with pretended homage.

debates: Whether this epistle was addressed to Ephesus, and what the absence of personal names implies.
Whether the closing word describes a love that cannot decay or a lover free from hypocrisy.
Whether peace here is the customary greeting or a prayer for concord in the church.
What authority the subscriptions and the closing Amen carry.
outliers: Clarke alone names the two scholars on either side of the question of the epistle's address, and concedes that the objection against Ephesus stands unanswered.
Ellicott alone reaches the same doubt from the impersonal wording of the benediction rather than from the absence of names.
Ellicott alone observes that this epistle's closing salutation is uniquely made conditional.
Calvin alone turns the warning against hypocrisy into a complaint about the professing religion of his own day.
Barnes alone leaves the exposition to address his reader about the close of his own life.
